I have sat on four boards, and I have watched hundreds of presentations. What I want to hear in the first minute is the request. Not the history of the project, not the market, not the team. What do you want this board to approve today? If I have to wait until slide nine to find out, I have already stopped listening. The best deck I ever saw had six slides. The presenter told us what she needed, why it mattered, what it would cost, and what we would get back. Then she sat down and waited for questions. And the questions are the real presentation. When a director asks you something hostile, it is not personal. What that director is doing is testing whether you believe your own proposal. So do not defend yourself. Answer the question, and bring it back to what you are asking for.

My first board presentation was a disaster, and I still think about it. I had prepared for two weeks. I had forty slides, and I spent the first fifteen minutes setting the scene: the regulation, the history, the risks in other countries. Then one of the directors raised his hand and asked me, very politely, what exactly I wanted from them. I did not have a one-sentence answer. I had a forty-slide answer. I could see the room losing interest, and I never got it back. They postponed the decision to the next meeting. What I should have done was start with the request. Now I do it every time. The first sentence is what I need, and the reason comes after it. The background goes at the end, and if nobody asks for it, I never show it at all.

First, the legal team gets ten minutes on the agenda of the next board meeting. Before he prepares a single slide, Pedro writes the request in one sentence. Then he cuts the slide deck from twenty slides to six. A week before the meeting, he rehearses with a colleague who asks him the most hostile questions she can think of. On the day, he opens with the request in one sentence, and the board approves a six-month pilot.
